title: Textures, signals and tables
summary: Edit an expression, connect a control signal, and use a table as a parameter source.

steps.title: One graph, three interfaces
steps.text: TOP carries images, CHOP carries sampled channels, and DAT carries documents and tables. The lesson workflow uses real nodes you can keep editing.

steps.title: Write a texture expression
steps.text: Change the expression, for example change x*12 to x*8. CodeMirror applies it while typing. The GPU program recompiles only when its source changes.

steps.title: Change a signal
steps.text: Adjust oscillator frequency. The FLOAT output is the last sample of its first channel; the channel output carries the whole named block.

steps.title: A FLOAT becomes a texture control
steps.text: Follow the wire from chop.lag to top.transform rotate. These are regular Comfy input sockets; signals update the live shader without a Python queue.

steps.title: A table becomes a parameter
steps.text: Edit a number in the table. dat.cell selects one cell and exposes it as STRING and FLOAT. The lesson wires its FLOAT into top.math value.

steps.title: GPU composition and history
steps.text: Inspect feedback, corner pin and compositing. Feedback keeps two GPU textures and avoids cyclic graph wires. Its history exists in Live mode; Queue returns the current input.

steps.title: Keep 3D in Three.js
steps.text: The Three.js Livecode source uses the same IMAGE path. Its code can read inputTexture and declared CHOP-driven parameters; no separate geometry engine is needed.

steps.title: Read and export the report
steps.text: The DAT document contains the library report. Use its export controls for Markdown, standalone HTML, or Print / Save as PDF. The report describes performance and device boundaries.

title: Preview and presentation
summary: Freeze only the node view, open an overlay, and present the final image.

steps.title: Local preview and workflow output
steps.text: Freeze the image preview. Its downstream stream continues; only this view holds the last frame.

steps.title: Use a floating overlay
steps.text: Select the preview node and press Alt+W, or use its overlay button. Alt+W also closes the overlay when you hover it. The last position is remembered.

steps.title: Fill the Comfy window
steps.text: Alt+F fills the Comfy viewport and restores it on a second press. It does not invoke macOS fullscreen. Browser fullscreen remains separate. Escape restores a filled overlay.

steps.title: Try a backdrop
steps.text: With this node selected and the editor unfocused, press D to toggle the graph backdrop. Alt+P hides node/code visibility while renderers keep running.

steps.title: Performance has more than one clock
steps.text: Comfy corner FPS measures graph redraw. The preview statistics measure delivered image frames. CHOP Hz describes sample time. These are different metrics.

title: MIDI and OSC controls
summary: Understand explicit device start and the realtime/queue boundary.

steps.title: MIDI stays user-started
steps.text: MIDI In/Out uses Web MIDI. Press Connect only when you are ready to grant the browser permission and choose a real device. Empty device text chooses the first port; an exact device name or ID selects one.

steps.title: Select the control you need
steps.text: CC and note values normalize to 0..1. Use chop.select patterns such as ch1.cc7 before mapping a FLOAT into an image or Livecode parameter.

steps.title: OSC stays on loopback
steps.text: OSC In listens on 127.0.0.1 only after Connect. OSC Out sends latest numeric channel values only after Connect. Ports and addresses remain ordinary Comfy controls.

steps.title: Queue never opens devices
steps.text: In Queue, MIDI/OSC In returns a zero placeholder and Out passes channels through without sending. Use Live mode for actual devices. Disconnect when done; abandoned OSC leases expire.

title: Make a tutorial with Genereti
summary: Record selections and actions, add hints, replay demonstrations and export a guided lesson.

steps.title: A lesson is a workflow document
steps.text: The dat.lesson node holds your guide JSON in CodeMirror. Its toolbar runs the learner dialogue and exports the document. The learner dialogue only navigates the lesson.
steps.hint: Use Focus to locate the tool, then follow the step instructions.

steps.title: Give your lesson an identity
steps.text: Change the title in the sample guide JSON. Use a unique id when you make another lesson, and keep format genereti-guide and version 1. All steps need a title and text.
steps.hint: Use Focus to locate the tool, then follow the step instructions.

steps.title: Describe a learner action
steps.text: Edit the first step text to give a concrete action and explain what should change. Narration is plain text; it never executes scripts or starts devices.
steps.hint: Use Focus to locate the tool, then follow the step instructions.

steps.title: Record a demonstration
steps.text: On dat.lesson press ● Record tutorial actions. Add or remove a node, select the texture expression node, edit its code or width/height, and connect nodes. Click/drag gestures are visual cues; values and connections are semantic actions. Device start, queue and arbitrary UI clicks are not replayed. The starting patch, node layout and titles are recorded too.
steps.hint: The filled circle starts recording. It does not run a learner guide.

steps.title: Split the recording into teaching steps
steps.text: Press + New recorded step after a coherent action. Then select another tool and type into its field. Press ✓ Stop recording and append steps to put your recording in the lesson JSON. Existing authored steps stay intact.
steps.hint: Use one step per idea. Intermediate slider values are coalesced; finish a gesture before pressing +.

steps.title: Add a hint and review the actions
steps.text: Each recorded step has editable title, text, hint, target and actions. Replace draft narration with a learner task; hint should explain a recovery path. type-text reveals text progressively; pointer cues visualize clicks and drags at normalized locations.
steps.hint: Add "hint": "Try changing the frequency first" inside a step. Hint never runs actions.

steps.title: Try Hint and Do it
steps.text: Run your guide. Hint reveals advice. Do it replays only the current step, visibly types committed text, changes real parameter values and restores recorded wiring. Next stays learner-controlled. Play all replays successive steps and pauses at manual instructions. Source auto-update is paused while typing; a recorded Livecode Run compiles afterward. Audio/capture stays explicitly activated.
steps.hint: The sample lesson already includes Hint and Do it examples. Run authored lesson replaces this authoring tour with your draft.

steps.title: Focus a real tool
steps.text: Targets use stable internal node types. Record captures a persistent ref and nodeId so two tools of the same type remain distinct. part can be node, code, preview, toolbar or parameter; widget names a parameter or editor.
steps.hint: Use Focus to locate the tool, then follow the step instructions.

steps.title: Try the check yourself
steps.text: Change this texture expression. A changed-widget check compares its value to the value at step entry, then enables Next. Learners can skip checks; this does not grade artistic quality.
steps.hint: Use Focus to locate the tool, then follow the step instructions.

steps.title: Export from the author toolbar
steps.text: Use Document export on dat.lesson for Markdown, standalone HTML, or Print / Save as PDF. Use {} for editable lesson JSON. Save the Comfy workflow separately to keep its nodes and wiring. Exports are deliberately outside the learner dialogue.
steps.hint: Use Focus to locate the tool, then follow the step instructions.

steps.title: Run and share your draft
steps.text: Press Run authored lesson on dat.lesson to register and play your edited guide. That replaces this walkthrough with your own learner dialogue. Stop ends playback without undoing edits. Sharing the workflow supplies the actual tools; sharing HTML/PDF supplies static notes.
steps.hint: Use Focus to locate the tool, then follow the step instructions.

title: Interactive output views
summary: Present a working sketch or document without losing interaction.

steps.title: Use the sketch
steps.text: Click the p5 output; its click counter changes. The moving circle follows your pointer.

steps.title: Hide just the node chrome
steps.text: Select p5 and press Alt+O, or Shift-click its overlay button. Only output remains. Hover just outside an edge to reveal its opacity and stacking controls. The restore glyph brings the chrome back.

steps.title: Move it into an overlay
steps.text: Restore the node, then press Alt+W or click the overlay button normally. The same sketch moves into an interactive overlay.

steps.title: Arrange two views
steps.text: Open the scrollable document overlay too. Hover a view and use Cmd+[ / ] for backward/forward, or Cmd+Shift+[ / ] for back/front. The bar has the same controls; Shift-click a stacking arrow for back/front. Code editors keep their own bracket shortcuts.

steps.title: Annotate and present
steps.text: The drawing node keeps the active editor in both views. Alt+Shift+O toggles click-through. Alt+F fills an overlay inside Comfy; Alt+P hides graph/code and Alt+Shift+Z hides the outer Comfy shell. Native browser fullscreen remains separate.
The expression draws fresh white dots on opaque black. This branch goes directly to the composite image input.
steps.title: Fresh source

steps.text: top.feedbackref picks the final composite as its reference. It copies that output on the GPU and exposes it on the next graph tick. No cyclic IMAGE cable is needed. The optional image input seeds the first frame; otherwise it begins transparent.
steps.title: Read the previous final image

steps.text: Multiply RGB by 0.96 to fade older marks. Try 0 to remove trails or 0.99 for longer history. Alpha is preserved, so decay affects visible brightness.
steps.title: Decay the history

steps.text: Transform the preceding composite before mixing it with fresh dots. You can insert blur, corner pin or other processors anywhere along this branch.
steps.title: Process the delayed frame

steps.text: Screen combines fresh dots with transformed history: black lets the trails show through. Over would cover history because this source is opaque. The reference targets this final composite; picking the original source instead gives a one-frame delay without recursive accumulation.
steps.title: Composite with the source

steps.text: Alt-W opens the final view; Alt-F fills the window. For a convenient single-node effect use top.feedback, which retains its own history and offers screen/add/over. Convert the reference STRING field to an input to drive it from a primitive or DAT. Camera, screen and audio still require explicit activation.
steps.title: Perform and experiment

title: A flexible feedback loop
summary: Use a delayed node reference to make a flexible recursive GPU feedback chain.

steps.text: Each RGB channel has a separate c index: 0 red, 1 green, 2 blue. Phase offsets give the dots different colors. This expression uses the same moving shape mask for all channels.
steps.title: Make a colored source
steps.hint: Use c in the color term, but leave it out of the shape mask. Try changing 24 to 16; Do it restores the colored-dot formula and 512 × 384 resolution.

steps.text: The source IMAGE seeds top.feedbackref. Its picker targets the final composite, so each frame samples the completed image from the preceding graph tick. Clear delayed reference frame resets it back to the seed. No cyclic IMAGE wire is needed.
steps.title: Seed and reference feedback
steps.hint: Connect the dots to the image seed, then choose the final screen composite in the reference picker. The reference samples the previous frame; do not draw a cyclic IMAGE cable.

steps.text: Threshold selects bright marks. A separable Gaussian blur spreads their light; strength adds the glow. Change radius to alter the displacement map softness. This is a compact four-pass GPU bloom, not an exact replica of TD bloom.
steps.title: Bloom the history
steps.hint: Connect feedback to bloom. Start with threshold 0.4, radius 16 and strength 0.8. A lower threshold spreads more of the history into the displacement map.

steps.text: The delayed image connects to image, and its bloomed copy connects to displacement. Red moves horizontal sampling and green moves vertical sampling relative to center 0.5. Try smaller amounts first; outside is transparent.
steps.title: Displace the previous frame
steps.hint: Use feedback as the image and bloom as the displacement map. Begin with 0.01 on both axes and center 0.5; larger amounts quickly distort the trail.

steps.text: Multiply history RGB by 0.98 to fade it, and set fresh input level around 0.4. Screen composite combines both branches. Reference the composite to accumulate a recursive trail; reference the original source for a simple delayed effect.
steps.title: Balance old and fresh images
steps.hint: Use multiply 0.98 on the displaced history and level 0.4 on the fresh source. Connect history to background and fresh marks to image on a screen composite.

steps.text: top.channels can extract alpha or luminance, swap RGB, or combine A with B channels such as br/bg/bb/ba. B here is the bloom. RGB uses opaque GPU alpha and returns a three-channel queued IMAGE; RGBA uses the alpha selector. Live texture storage remains RGBA.
steps.title: Route and combine channels
steps.hint: A is the composite; B is bloom. Try red=b or green=bg to remix the color. Do it restores r/g/b with opaque alpha and RGB output.

steps.text: Alt-W opens the interactive output, Alt-F fills the window. Clear delayed reference frame resets the loop without reconstructing the graph. top.feedback remains the convenient self-contained variant. Audio, camera and screen remain explicitly user-started.
steps.title: Present and experiment
steps.hint: Connect the routed channels to the viewer. Do it opens its output overlay; then use Alt-F to fill the window and Escape to restore it.

summary: Reproduce the reference-based feedback lesson with independent GPU operators.
title: Class patch: feedback, bloom and displacement

steps.hint: Use Do it for this step, or Play remaining to build the sequence. Click any outline title to revisit a step.
steps.text: Create a texture expression and connect it to temporal feedback. No cyclic cable is needed: top.feedback stores the preceding frame internally. Screen blending is the default so opaque black lets older trails show through; over requires transparent source frames.

steps.hint: Use Do it for this step, or Play remaining to build the sequence. Click any outline title to revisit a step.
steps.text: Add the image viewer, tune decay/rotation and insert an invert filter. Edit decay gently to balance fresh shapes with trails.

steps.hint: Use Do it for this step, or Play remaining to build the sequence. Click any outline title to revisit a step.
steps.text: Build a 96 BPM transport, melodic note sequence and FM voice. Audio remains stopped while the patch is assembled.

steps.title: Test a processor and tidy the patch

steps.hint: This step is manual because device and audio activation are explicit gestures.
steps.text: Playback pauses here. Press Start on mod.output explicitly, then listen and adjust the melody, cutoff and mixer. Watch the feedback viewer; Alt-W opens its overlay, Alt-F fills the window. Stop/Panic ends the audio. Save the patch and record another variation with the lesson toolbar.
steps.title: Start and test the performance

summary: A luminous abstract performance stage made from hand-cut paper shapes, cobalt blue and orange light, energetic theatrical composition. A recorded, model-free patch-building session.
title: Build a feedback AV synth

steps.hint: Try simplex, 3 dimensions, scale 8, 3 octaves and seed 12. RGB offsets the channels to give independent color.
steps.text: top.noise generates live GPU textures. Its seed offsets the noise domain; octaves layer finer detail with normalized amplitude.
steps.title: Layer a simplex texture

steps.hint: Switch to 4 dimensions, z 0.5 and speed 0.2. Change z to explore a different slice.
steps.text: 1D is a varying stripe; 2D is a plane. In 3D, time moves through depth. In 4D, z selects a volume slice and time has its own axis. Set speed to zero to hold the field.
steps.title: Choose dimensionality

steps.hint: Use x/y for spatial coordinates, t for evolution and c to offset RGB channels. This panel shows 3D Perlin.
steps.text: noise is an alias for perlin. perlin, simplex and value accept 1–4 coordinates and return signed values. Map to display range with 0.5+0.5*noise(...). CHOP expressions share these functions.
steps.title: Write a noise expression

steps.hint: Do it opens the layered noise viewer. Explore value noise or connect the result as a displacement map in the class feedback patch.
steps.text: The viewer receives a GPU texture. Alt-W opens its output overlay; Alt-F fills the window. Queue samples the explicit time parameter.
steps.title: Present the result

summary: Compare layered simplex textures with per-channel Perlin expressions.
title: Coherent noise: textures and expressions
Paint with noise and reference feedback
summary: A luminous abstract performance stage made from hand-cut paper shapes, cobalt blue and orange light, energetic theatrical composition. Model-free pigment, grain and brush-flow feedback; includes Hint, Do it and cursor demonstrations.

steps.title: Grow a broad noise field
steps.text: Start with 3D simplex noise: x/y make the field, the slowly moving third coordinate animates it. Scale changes the size of the pigment regions. Do it builds this step; Play remaining builds the whole patch.
steps.hint: Choose Live, 512 × 320, simplex, 3 dimensions, scale 3, speed 0.02. The cursor paths here are authored demonstrations; Record captures your own paths.

steps.title: Color and grain the fresh paint
steps.text: The expression maps grayscale noise to eight warm/cool pigment bands. Fine value noise is added at low opacity. Image is A; background is B: add gives B + opacity × A.
steps.hint: Connect broad noise → expression. Connect palette → composite background, fine grain → image. Opacity 0.055 keeps the grain subtle. c selects RGB; v is the incoming component.

steps.title: Prepare a delayed frame and brush flow
steps.text: feedbackref is a delay, not a composite. Its IMAGE input seeds the first frame. Its output must feed a processing chain to influence the result. Leave reference empty until we make the final target. A colored noise map supplies different red/green displacement directions.
steps.hint: Connect fresh pigment → feedbackref image. Make another simplex noise with RGB color, scale 5 and speed 0.012. The reference target comes in step 5.

steps.title: Process the previous paint
steps.text: Move the delayed frame with the flow map, then soften it with a small blur. These processors sit inside the feedback loop, so their effect accumulates each frame.
steps.hint: feedbackref → displace image; RGB noise → displace displacement; displace → blur. Start with X/Y 0.01 and radius 0.7 pixels.

actions.title: ꘇ top.displace · brush the old paint

steps.title: Close the loop with a reference
steps.text: Crossfade fresh pigment (image A) with processed history (background B). At opacity 0.06 the result is 6% fresh + 94% old. Set feedbackref reference to the final composite named REF TARGET. That dashed logical link reads the previous completed frame; no cyclic IMAGE cable is needed. Referencing the fresh source instead would only delay it.
steps.hint: Wire fresh → final composite image, blur → background. In feedbackref’s picker choose “painted result / REF TARGET”. The final composite is the target, not the seed. Use the reset arrow to clear history.

actions.title: ꘇ top.composite · painted result / REF TARGET

steps.title: Present and record a variation
steps.text: Open the canvas overlay with Alt-W; Alt-F fills the browser window. Increase fresh opacity for faster renewal, reduce it for longer brush memory. Change flow scale/speed for different marks. Record on dat.lesson captures named parameter changes and cursor paths; + separates steps, Stop saves them. Review its JSON before exporting or sharing.
steps.hint: Select the viewer for Alt-W. In the lesson toolbar press Record, drag a float parameter, hover between controls and click; stop recording and replay the new step. Audio, camera and screen capture remain manual.

title: See sound, use sound
summary: Scopes, spectral analysis, stereo geometry and audio-driven visual controls.

steps.title: Start the patch
steps.text: Press ▷ on mod.output. Sound starts explicitly at a low level. The analysis taps remain silent until their source is part of a running output patch.
steps.hint: Use Start on the output, not Queue or the lesson Play button.

steps.title: Read the waveform
steps.text: mod.scope draws left and right waveforms. Its channels output carries sampled stereo data; image carries the drawing. RMS and peak sockets are scalar controls.
steps.hint: Increase display_gain to enlarge the drawing without changing sound.

steps.title: Read the spectrum
steps.text: mod.spectrum draws decibels on a linear-frequency axis. Channels are magnitude and frequency in Hz. fft_size trades frequency detail for a longer analysis window; smoothing affects spectral bins only.
steps.hint: The frequency of bin i is i × sampleRate / fft_size.

steps.title: See stereo relationships
steps.text: mod.lissajous plots left versus right. A centered mono signal forms a diagonal. Change pan to stretch it; richer stereo effects can create loops. Correlation is +1 for identical signals, -1 for opposite phase.
steps.hint: Pan changes balance, not phase; it will tilt a line rather than generate a loop.

steps.title: Use analysis as controls
steps.text: mod.analyze exposes rms, peak, correlation and low/mid/high spectral band amplitudes. chop.select chooses rms, chop.math multiplies it by 12, and its FLOAT output drives the opacity of the scope image in top.filter.
steps.hint: Follow channels → select rms → math → FLOAT amount. These are control-rate measurements, not an audio-rate CHOP DSP engine.

steps.title: Stop and save
steps.text: Press ■ Panic on mod.output. Analysis and scalar controls return to zero. Save retains wiring and settings, never a playing AudioContext.
steps.hint: Queue returns silent analysis data and placeholder IMAGEs; the browser owns live analysis.

title: Livecode: shader buffers and history
summary: Connected GLSL passes, one-frame history and an explicit fresh/history composite.

steps.title: Make fresh ink
steps.text: The first GLSL node paints moving RGB ink. Each Livecode node is a separate render pass. Change speed without rebuilding the shader.
steps.hint: mainImage, iTime, iResolution and iChannel0 aliases are supported. Annotated float speed becomes a regular parameter and controls.value0 socket.

steps.title: Reference the end of the loop
steps.text: Buffer A reads the previous composite. Its optional IMAGE input seeds frame one; it does not choose the history target. Pick the combine node in reference.
steps.hint: Fresh → composite; previous composite → warp/fade → composite. The reference closes the loop with a one-tick delay, so there is no cyclic IMAGE wire.

steps.title: Process the history buffer
steps.text: The warp pass samples its IMAGE input as iChannel0 / u_image. It rotates, expands and fades yesterday’s pixels before they reach the composite.
steps.hint: Lower decay shortens trails. Here one input is one external buffer; internal Shadertoy A–D/Common tabs and four channel inputs are not implemented.

steps.title: Combine fresh and old frames
steps.text: Add fresh RGB ink to faded history. Display grading comes after the composite so it cannot amplify history each tick.
steps.hint: Screen is another useful blend. Over with an opaque black source would hide history. Do it restores additive routing.

steps.title: Finish and interact
steps.text: Increase contrast in the Image pass. Alt+W opens the actual interactive preview; Shift-click its overlay button or Alt+O keeps only the node output.
steps.hint: IMAGE between Livecode nodes crosses separate browser runtimes. TOP operators keep their own GPU chain. Use dat.monitor on your actual patch rather than assuming a fixed frame rate.

title: Livecode: two p5 sketches, one image stream
summary: An interactive source feeds a mirrored tile processor using inputImage.

steps.title: Draw in the source
steps.text: The left sketch paints animated colored dots. Press and move inside its output to paint a larger light spot. Its mouse is local to this source runtime.
steps.hint: Use the output below the editor, Alt+W or Alt+O. Enable interaction in the overlay if you turned click-through on. Do it slows the animation, then try the mouse yourself.

steps.title: Pass pixels to another sketch
steps.text: Connect the source IMAGE to the processor image input. The processor receives inputImage, a p5.Image refreshed as frames arrive.
steps.hint: inputImage is null before the first frame. It is an image, not the other sketch’s variables or canvas DOM. Do it reconnects the two sketches.

steps.title: Tile without recompiling
steps.text: tiles is an annotated number. Change its regular control to resize the grid; the same image is drawn into alternating mirrored cells.
steps.hint: The code rounds tiles to an integer. controls.value0 is the stable socket ID; tiles is its friendly label.

steps.title: Edit independent runtimes
steps.text: Each sketch has its own setup, draw, frameCount and pointer. The downstream node receives images, not source code. Save keeps source text and wiring.
steps.hint: Do it restores a leisurely source speed. You can add another Livecode p5 node and keep extending this image pipeline.

steps.title: Present the processed output
steps.text: Open the viewer or processor as an overlay. Source interaction continues to appear in the tiled output; keep the source preview accessible when performing.
steps.hint: Alt+W makes a floating view; Alt+O hides node chrome. Each node’s Queue capture freezes its current output; neither creates a shared p5 runtime.

title: Livecode: sound analysis becomes visual control
summary: A quiet modular synth, RMS signal routing, spectrum/scope and an interactive p5 display.

steps.title: Start sound explicitly
steps.text: Press ▷ Start on mod.output at its low level. The lesson Play/Do it controls never unlock audio; this step waits for your own audio gesture.
steps.hint: The music clock and sequence describe notes; the output activates the browser AudioContext. Panic stops it. Queue never plays sound.

steps.title: Inspect the sound
steps.text: scope shows stereo waveforms, spectrum shows frequency-bin magnitudes, and lissajous plots left against right. Display gain enlarges drawings without changing sound.
steps.hint: fft_size trades frequency detail for a longer analysis window. Do it sets 2048; all three taps analyze the running gain bus.

steps.title: Route RMS into p5
steps.text: analyze.channels → chop.select rms → chop.math × 12 → energy. FLOAT is the last sample of the named control block. The p5 rings grow with sound level.
steps.hint: This is control-rate analysis, not audio-rate DSP. energy is clamped to 0..1 in the annotated parameter. Do it restores the connection and increases sensitivity.

steps.title: Add a pointer to the performance
steps.text: Hold and move the pointer inside the p5 output. Light spots follow your mouse while ring size follows audio. Both interactions stay live in Alt+W / Alt+O.
steps.hint: Do it changes the unconnected sensitivity parameter. The connected energy default is overridden by RMS, so changing its local widget cannot defeat the wire.

steps.title: Explore stereo and stop
steps.text: Adjust pan to tilt the lissajous line. Mono balance is not phase modulation. Press Panic on mod.output when finished; analysis and energy return to zero.
steps.hint: Do it only changes pan. Stop audio yourself. A future stereo effect can turn the diagonal into a loop; this demo preserves the actual channel relationship.
